newsitem.title: BOSNIA: West must get tough in Bosnia to keep peace - agency.
newsitem.headline: West must get tough in Bosnia to keep peace - agency.

text.p: Western troops must seek out indicted war criminals in Bosnia as a key step to securing a lasting peace, an international monitoring agency said on Tuesday.

Without such urgent measures Bosnia faces renewed war, the International Crisis Group (ICG), a private monitoring commission with broad international membership, said in a report prepared for a major London conference to review the peace.

"The conflict has by no means been resolved and may spill over into bloodshed again," said the report. It pointed to the failure of peace provisions designed to remove ethnic barriers as the basis for its pessimism.

Foreign ministers from Europe, North America and Russia meet in Britain on Wednesday and Thursday to assess progress in former Yugoslavia. They were not expected to go beyond urging all sides to reaffirm their commitment to previous accords.
The ICG twinned its gloomy assessment of Bosnia's prospects for peace with a call for practical steps to salvage the November 1995 Dayton accords that ended 43 months of war.
First on its list was a call to NATO's governing council to order the thousands of alliance troops in Bosnia to actively seek out the dozens of indicted war criminals still at large.

Led by the United States, the 50,000-strong peace force, soon to be cut to 30,000, has shied from the risky task of capturing wanted men, fearing casualties that will be unpopular and politically costly at home.

"There cannot be reconciliation without accountability," said Hrair Balian, director of ICG's Bosnia operation. Only seven out of 74 indictees have been captured so far and world enthusiasm for the war crimes process has appeared to wane.

Millions of dollars of reconstruction aid should be withheld and their release linked to the participation of reluctant Bosnian Serbs, Croats and Moslems in joint governing bodies meant to knit the country together, the report says.
Without strict "conditionality" aid will be wasted, it says. "It's the only real leverage we've got," said Balian.

Authorities who harbour wanted men, including the governments of Croatia and Serbia, should suffer financially, while communities who welcome back refugees from all ethnic groups should be rewarded, the report suggests.

The right of refugees to return home was a cornerstone of the peace deal but only 250,000 have managed, and those almost entirely to their own ethnic areas. Almost all moves to reestablish mixed ethnic communities in Bosnia have foundered.
Little money has been spent in the Bosnian Serb republic. Balian said new moves to ignore the actions of the separatist Serb leadership and quicken the flow of cash were foolish.
"All the signs are there that a wedge is being driven between the (Serb) leadership, which is seen as responsible for economic non-development, and the population," he said.
The ICG also called for greater efforts to ensure next year's municipal polls are free and fair after this September's national election, which it described as deeply flawed.
The ICG earned widespread respect in August when it helped unveil mass manipulation of voter registration.
Balian acknowledged the ICG's demands for tougher action may well go unheeded by Western politicians fearful of deeper military involvement in Bosnia.
"I don't know if the NATO mandate will change but we have to ask for it," he said. "We are pressing on a broad front. These are all make or break issues for the peace agreement."
